what_its_for: Adalimumab-bwwd is used to reduce inflammation and treat several conditions including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis (spine arthritis), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, plaque psoriasis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation and can damage your joints and tissues.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin, usually in your thigh or belly (at least 2 inches away from your belly button). Do not inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or hard. Rotate your injection sites each time. You can give yourself the shot at home after your doctor or nurse teaches you how. The medicine comes as a prefilled pen or syringe. Let the pen or syringe warm up at room temperature for 15 to 30 minutes before injecting — do not heat it up in a microwave or hot water. Clean the injection site with an alcohol wipe and let it dry before injecting.
dosing: Your dose and how often you take it depends on the condition being treated. Common dosing schedules include every other week (every 14 days) for many adult conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and plaque psoriasis. Some conditions like Crohn's disease may start with a higher starting dose and then switch to a maintenance dose. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, give it as soon as you remember. Then go back to your regular schedule. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue on your regular schedule. Do not give two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store adalimumab-bwwd in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it, and do not use it if it has been frozen. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days in its original carton — once removed from the refrigerator, write the date on the carton and throw it away after 14 days even if it has not been used. Do not shake the pen or syringe. Keep out of reach of children. Dispose of used needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container right away.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine lowers your immune system and makes it harder to fight infections. Avoid live vaccines (such as the nasal flu vaccine, MMR, chickenpox vaccine) while taking this medication — talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid excessive sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine may slightly increase your risk of skin cancer. Tell your doctor if you plan to become pregnant, are pregnant, or are breastfeeding before using this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath, burning when you urinate, or open sores on your body. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of your face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Contact your doctor if you experience chest pain, numbness or tingling, vision changes, unusual bruising or bleeding, extreme tiredness, or new or worsening symptoms. This medicine can increase the risk of serious infections including tuberculosis (TB) and certain fungal infections, as well as rare cancers — report any unusual lumps, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss right away.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your symptoms within 2 to 12 weeks of starting treatment, but it may take up to 3 to 6 months to feel the full benefit of this medicine. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better. Stopping and restarting this medicine can increase your risk of reactions.
special_populations: Children: This medicine can be used in children as young as 2 years old for certain conditions such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis and plaque psoriasis — the dose is based on the child's weight. Elderly patients: Older adults may have a higher risk of infections while taking this medicine — your doctor will monitor you closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. If you used this medicine during pregnancy, tell your baby's doctor before your baby receives any live vaccines, as the medicine can pass to the baby and may affect their immune system for several months after birth. Talk to your doctor if you are breastfeeding. People with TB or hepatitis B: Your doctor will test you for tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting this medicine, as it can reactivate these infections.
